title: VOYAGER: An Open-Ended Embodied Agent with Large Language Models
problem_statement: How can an embodied agent continuously acquire, accumulate, and reuse skills in an open-ended environment without human intervention or model parameter fine-tuning?
key_ideas: Represent skills as executable code (JavaScript/Mineflayer) rather than natural language or weight updates
Index skill programs by semantic embeddings for similarity-based retrieval
Use a GPT-4-driven automatic curriculum that adapts bottom-up to the agent's current capability frontier
Iterative prompting with three feedback types: environment state feedback, execution errors, and LLM-based self-verification
Skill library as an external, persistent, portable memory — separable from any specific agent or model
method_summary: VOYAGER consists of three components: (1) an automatic curriculum where GPT-4 proposes tasks based on agent state + exploration history, targeting diversity; (2) a skill library — a vector DB mapping GPT-3.5 embeddings of program descriptions to JavaScript programs, with retrieval by embedding similarity; (3) an iterative prompting loop with environment feedback, execution errors, and self-verification (separate GPT-4 critic), up to 4 rounds per task. No gradient-based training; GPT-4 and GPT-3.5 used as blackbox APIs.
metrics: Prompting iterations to unlock tech tree tiers (wooden/stone/iron/diamond)
Zero-shot task success rate and iterations on 4 unseen tasks

key_results.unique_items: 63 items in 160 iterations vs ~19 for best baseline (3.3x)
key_results.tech_tree_diamond: 102 iterations (1/3 runs) — only VOYAGER reaches diamond
key_results.zero_shot: VOYAGER solves all 4 tasks 3/3 runs; all baselines fail 0/3
key_results.gpt4_vs_gpt35: GPT-4 gets 5.7x more unique items than GPT-3.5

contributions: First LLM-powered embodied lifelong learning agent operating without model fine-tuning
Skill library architecture: executable code + embedding-based retrieval as persistent procedural memory
Automatic curriculum driven by LLM world knowledge, adapting to agent state
Iterative prompting with environment feedback + execution errors + self-verification
Demonstrated skill library portability (AutoGPT + VOYAGER skills improves AutoGPT)
limitations_acknowledged: GPT-4 API cost is 15x GPT-3.5; GPT-3.5 too weak for code generation quality needed
Agent occasionally gets stuck and fails to generate correct skill
Hallucinations: curriculum proposes non-existent items; code generation calls non-existent APIs
Self-verification module occasionally fails on ambiguous success signals
Text-only: no visual perception at time of writing
limitations_observed: No skill pruning or quality control — library grows unboundedly; retrieval quality at scale untested
Zero-shot evaluation only on 4 craft tasks; no spatial or biome-novel tasks
No comparison against gradient-based continual learners (DreamerV3, VPT) on same metrics
Curriculum quality depends on GPT-4 knowledge of Minecraft; unclear generalization to less-documented domains
relevance_to_thesis: Directly relevant to all three focus areas. Skill library = concrete procedural memory architecture (external, embedding-indexed, executable). Plug-and-play skill transfer to AutoGPT = inter-agent knowledge transfer demonstration. No-weight-update learning = important data point for defining educability: does it require weight updates or is external skill accumulation sufficient?
gaps_and_questions: Does a skill library built with GPT-4 transfer to Claude/Llama (cross-model skill transfer)?
Can this architecture generalize beyond Minecraft to research or API workflows?
What happens to retrieval quality as library scales to 100s or 1000s of skills?
Skill acquisition rate as a function of base model could operationalize educability metrics
Comparison: executable-code skills vs. natural-language descriptive memories (Generative Agents) — which transfers better?
poc_ideas: Port skill library to a research assistant domain: skills = Python/API functions, curriculum = GPT-4 proposes research subtasks, retrieval by embedding similarity
Cross-model transfer test: accumulate 50 skills with GPT-4, measure zero-shot task completion with Claude and Llama-3 using same skill library
Educability benchmark: fix curriculum and tasks, vary base model, measure iterations-to-proficiency curve
